item.title: A detailed verification of Neary's PCP(5) construction
item.description: arXiv:2611.29559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neary proved that the Post correspondence problem remains undecidable for instances with five pairs of words. We give a detailed verification of his construction. We first verify the undecidability of the restricted binary tag-system halting problem used in the reduction. We then prove both directions of the reduction to the five-pair problem, using the longer closing pair proposed by Rote. In particular, we show that every solution of the constructed PCP instance yields a halting computation of the simulated tag system.
item.dc:creator: Vesa Halava

item.title: Complexity of the Infinity and the Modulo-Counting Quantifiers in Automatic Structures
item.description: arXiv:2611.30944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic structures allow us to decide their first-order theory using automata-theoretic techniques. The complexity of this decision problem for formulas in prenex normal form depends on the quantifier alternation depth, e.g., it is PSPACE-complete for formulas with quantifier-prefix $\exists\exists\cdots\exists$. Blumensath observed that the decidability also holds if one extends first-order logic with the infinity quantifier. His decision procedure introduces many more quantifier alternations such that, even for formulas with quantifier prefix $\exists^\infty\exists^\infty\cdots\exists^\infty$ of length $n$, his decision procedure runs in $(2n-1)$-fold exponential space. We show that this is not necessary. To be more precise, we prove that handling the infinity quantifier is not more costly than handling the existential quantifier. On the other hand, we also show that addition of the modulo-counting quantifier to first-order logic results in a much higher complexity.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Klimmer, Dietrich Kuske, Sebastian Pfau

item.title: Rate--burst safety languages: the Farey structure of the burst boundary and discrimination under erasures
item.description: arXiv:2611.28606v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A leaky-bucket constraint with rate \(\rho\) and burst \(B\) allows at most \(\rho n+B\) costly steps in every window of \(n\) consecutive steps. The infinite 0/1 words that satisfy it form a safety language. For a finite graph with edge costs 0 and 1, we study the least burst at which the cost word of some infinite path lies in this language, as a function of the real rate. This function is the exact tolerance of a monitor that distinguishes two finite-state systems observed through an erasure channel with a leaky-bucket bound. The language is \(\omega\)-regular at every rational rate but not at irrational rates once the burst reaches 1, so ultimately periodic witnesses do not come from automata theory. We prove directly that simple lassos suffice at all real rates and that all breakpoints of the boundary lie in the Farey sequence of order N for a graph with N vertices. One lasso has a tight bound of order N to the power 2/3 on its affine pieces, whereas the choice among paths creates downward jumps and boundaries that are neither convex nor concave. One evaluation at the mediant of each Farey interval recovers the affine piece and an optimal lasso, and a greatest-fixed-point computation over decreasing integer bursts yields the whole function in polynomial time and linear working space. We also compute discrimination horizons and extend the Farey structure to turn-based safety games.
item.dc:creator: Lihui Dong, Zhuo Li

item.title: Characterizing normality via automata and random matrix products
item.description: arXiv:2604.12457v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a fixed alphabet A, an infinite sequence X is said to be normal if every word w over A appears in X with the same frequency as any other word of the same length. A classical result relates normality to finite automata as follows: a sequence X is normal if and only if all gambling strategies implementable with finite deterministic automata lose all their capital when trying to predict the next bit of X after seing the ones before. More precisely, Schnorr and Stimm (1972) proved that the capital goes exponentially fast to zero unless the automaton represents the gambler that never bets, in which case the capital remains constant. In this paper we show that an analogous result holds when considering probabilistic automata: a sequence X is normal if and only if for any gambling strategy implementable with probabilistic finite automaton it holds that the expected value of the capital of the gambler converges exponentially fast to a finite value when playing against X. To obtain this result, we show a more general statement related to the convergence of martingales given by finite sets of non-negative matrices {M a } a$\in$A . In particular, we show that X is normal if and only if ||vM X[1] . . . M X[n] || converges exponentially fast to a finite value for any non-negative starting vector v. Moreover, we distinguish three distinctive behaviours that this sequence can attain, and prove that the problem of recognizing, given a family of matrices, to which case it belongs, is decidable.
item.dc:creator: Laurent Bienvenu (CNRS, LaBRI), Santiago Cifuentes (ICC, UBA), Hugo Gimbert (CNRS, LaBRI)

item.title: Certified Split Points for Parallel Lexing: Exact and Modulo Discarded Tokens
item.description: arXiv:2608.03473v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Table-driven DFA lexing is sequential, since each transition depends on the previous byte's state. Scanning one input in parallel needs each chunk's entry state, which existing methods recover by simulation, speculation, prescanning, or overlap. We give two conditions under which none is needed. For a longest-match scanner restarting from q0 at every token boundary, a byte b is a certified split symbol when no reachable state other than q0 has a b-transition whose target can reach acceptance, and q0 is not re-entrant if it has one. Every occurrence of such a byte in completely tokenizable input begins a token, so chunks starting there reproduce the serial sequence of kinds and lengths. The condition is necessary and sufficient, but one string, comment, or whitespace run can remove every useful certificate. Comments and whitespace are usually discarded, so we weaken the guarantee to equality after deleting a declared discarded set and give a second condition, a precomputed constant-time one-bit test. It is sound but incomplete and more permissive, strictly so on suitable token and discarded sets. It recovers newline for a conventional C-like tokenization and tab, newline and carriage return for JSON, and refuses newline where block comments are unrestricted. Safety modulo the discarded set is PSPACE-complete for general token automata and decidable in polynomial time for literal vocabularies, and every unsafe byte has a replayable counterexample. On the fifteen token sets studied the second condition is already exact. Splitting at exact certificates in munch reaches 92.6-95.3% parallel efficiency at eight threads on a restricted CPU set and a 512 MiB corpus, and a 3.46-3.94x end-to-end speedup at four threads, on one machine. It turns delimiter-based parallel lexing from a language-specific assumption into a property a compiler checks.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: Certified Split Windows for Parallel Lexing: Recovering Boundaries Where No Byte Certifies
item.description: arXiv:2608.09761v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A certified split point lets a parallel lexer cut unlexed input at one byte with the serial token stream provably preserved, but several conventional token sets in the predecessor's study certify no byte once string, comment, or whitespace-run forms are included (arXiv:2608.03473v2). We generalize from a byte to a bounded window, a byte string such that, whatever the context, the token covering its final byte begins at a known origin. Since the certificate is conditional on occurrence and may be vacuous, every applicability figure counts only windows carrying an asserted completely tokenizable occurrence witness. We give a conservative model of a maximal-munch scanner's possible histories across a window, prove it sound, and decide reachability in it exactly by exhausting a finite quotient of its reachable configurations. Within the flat, completely tokenizable scope, model-positive answers are semantic certificates; negatives are relative to the model, which refuses some windows a greedy scanner would allow. For both model and semantic certificates, existence is PSPACE-complete with or without a witness requirement, and a shortest window has $2^{\Theta(n)}$ bytes in the worst case over at most $n$ live states. Two smaller searches decide plain model existence, the second shipped in release 2.2.0 of munch. Of 400 random token sets, 322 of the 337 certifying no byte gain witnessed windows and four more gain model certificates with occurrence unresolved. No model search reaches its threshold. The predecessor's exact-empty rows all gain witnessed windows of two to four bytes. A boundary profile marks each gap of an occurring window forced, crossed or open, and a window-local cut is sound exactly at forced gaps. Whether a given gap is ever a boundary and whether it is open are PSPACE-complete, while occurrence, the forced verdict and a given origin's certificate are NL-complete.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: Complete Test Suites for Effectful Automata
item.description: arXiv:2611.26535v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complete test suites for automata are (finite) sets of words that enable testing an implementation against a specification: when a (black-box) automaton passes the test suite, completeness guarantees that it is equivalent to the specification on all (infinitely many) words. A well-known method for constructing complete test suites for deterministic automata is the W-method, used in conformance testing and automata learning. Based on a recent categorical generalisation of the W-method, we propose a framework for~the construction and analysis of test suites for a certain class of effectful automata defined by commutative monads. By working in the Eilenberg-Moore category of the associated monad at hand, we obtain a generic notion of effectful W-method, together with a completeness theorem. We show how to apply the framework and derive complete test suites for non-deterministic and weighted automata.
item.dc:creator: B\'alint Kocsis, Rick Koenders, Joshua Moerman, Jurriaan Rot

item.title: Ensemble Logic
item.description: arXiv:2408.14443v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We interpret formulas over metric monoids, that is, commutative monoids equipped with translation-invariant metrics. Displacement evaluates a formula at a translated point, while bounded existence and bounded universality evaluate it at some or every point of a window of prescribed length. Quantification over points and lengths allows the same variable to occur in the parameters of several operators. This provides a common framework for temporal and spatial reasoning in discrete, dense and multi-dimensional settings. Our main result establishes a sharp undecidability boundary for satisfiability over the natural numbers: satisfiability is undecidable already for formulas $\exists N\,\exists n\,\Psi$ in which $\Psi$ is built from the letters of a fixed alphabet by conjunction, disjunction, displacement and bounded universality. We prove this by a reduction from Post's Correspondence Problem. We also present results, in part from companion work, that place this theorem in the general theory of EL. These include an atomic-displacement normal form for covariant windows and composition laws for discrete and dense time. The discrete logic admits an embedding of linear temporal logic, defines the accepting runs of every B\"uchi automaton, and has a sound equational calculus. For the rational logic, we show that every fixed formula can be evaluated in polynomial time on interval models in which atomic propositions are interpreted by finite unions of intervals. Finally, we represent timed words over positions and real time and compare two window geometries; with rectangular windows, two shared lengths yield undecidability on finite timed words.
item.dc:creator: Guo-Qiang Zhang

item.title: A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
item.description: arXiv:2411.19906v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: L-systems are widely used to model and simulate biological growth processes, including plant development. Motivated by the broader goal of automating L-system construction, this paper studies the formal deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) inference problem in which the input is a finite, noise-free sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a string sequence and prove that the existence of a compatible D0L-system is equivalent to the existence of an independent set of a prescribed size in this graph. This gives polynomial reductions from D0L inference to maximum independent set (MIS) and SAT, and hence an exact classical decision route when combined with an exact MIS or SAT solver. We also describe a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)-based quantum heuristic for generating candidate independent sets. This heuristic is not a decision procedure for D0L inference, and failure of the heuristic is inconclusive rather than a certificate of nonexistence. We include computational validation on $22$ generated D0L traces and $8$ negative controls, explicitly incorporate known fixed-identity symbols, and report small statevector QAOA simulations. The quantum component is presented as a proof-of-concept candidate generator, not as a claimed quantum speedup; the immediately useful contribution is the characteristic-graph reduction and the exact classical/SAT decision framework it enables.
item.dc:creator: Ali Lotfi, Ian McQuillan, Steven Rayan

item.title: Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2511.03752v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.
item.dc:creator: Rick van der Heijden

item.title: Cycle Counting and Character Expectations Using Alternating Structures
item.description: arXiv:2608.27593v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recently, three related papers [arXiv:2412.13941, arXiv:2009.00897, arXiv:2409.03626] found a connection between two subjects: the w-cycle theorem, which is a theorem about counting appearances of cycles reading out a word w in certain graphs, and character expectations on word measures. The w-cycle theorem was proven independently by [arXiv:1410.2540] using stackings and by [arXiv:1410.2579] using bislim structures. In the current work, we generalize stackings and bislim structures to alternating stackings and alternating bislim structures. We show how this significantly strengthens the w-cycle theorem for words admitting such alternating structures, and as a result, also strengthens the recent results of [arXiv:2412.13941] and [arXiv:2409.03626]. We show that generic words admit alternating bislim structures, and therefore, the strengthened results hold for generic words. Using our new machinery, we address conjectures of Wilton, of Hanany--Puder and of Puder--Shomroni. We prove that all three conjectures hold for generic words, but we also find counterexamples for the first two.
item.dc:creator: Noam Ta Shma

item.title: Constant-Coin Complete-Information Debates for $\mathsf{P}$ with Arbitrarily Small Strong Error
item.description: arXiv:2609.24272v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study complete-information debate systems in which a probabilistic finite-state verifier reads the alternating messages of a prover and a refuter. Demirci, Say, and Yakary{\i}lmaz showed that every language in $\mathsf{P}$ has such debates checkable with a constant number of random bits and arbitrarily small weak error. Their strong-error construction, which also counts nontermination as failure, did not permit arbitrary error reduction. We close this gap: for every $L\in\mathsf{P}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a constant-space verifier using a constant number of private coin tosses that has perfect completeness and strong error at most $\varepsilon$. The verifier simulates a polynomial-time alternating multihead finite automaton, privately spot-checking one of its input heads. The key observation is that, on a nonmember, the refuter may concede any round in which the prover first misreports a head reading. This ensures termination against every prover when the refuter follows the specified strategy, and permits strong-error reduction by repetition.
item.dc:creator: M. Utkan Gezer
